content: Since 2010, the following findings have been reported: Argentina: A bibliographic review conducted by Mera y Sierra and colleagues in 2011 identified 58 reports documenting 619 human cases of fascioliasis across 13 provinces. The first human case was reported in 1924. Most cases were concentrated in high-altitude regions, particularly in Catamarca, Mendoza, and San Luis. Interestingly, the distribution of human cases did not align with the distribution of animal cases. Only 3% of cases were detected using microscopy. Bolivia: During the 1990s and earlier, the Bolivian highlands near Lake Titicaca exhibited some of the highest global prevalence rates of fascioliasis, with a prevalence of 2%. In 2008, a pilot project in Huacullani used mass drug administration with triclabendazole (10 mg/kg), demonstrating the drug's safety and efficacy. Based on these results, Bolivia's Ministry of Health implemented annual mass drug administration programs in specific regions of La Paz from 2008 to 2021, excluding 2011, 2015, 2018, and 2020. Since 2010, only three publications have reported human prevalence data. For example, in 2017, a prevalence of 6% was reported in Pucarani, while no cases were detected in Viacha. Haiti: While animal fascioliasis has been documented in Haiti, no human cases were reported until 2012. A prevalence of 5% was detected using Western blot. However, the absence of coprological data makes it unclear whether the disease is endemic or sporadic. Mexico: Historically, human fascioliasis in Mexico was considered sporadic, with only 50 cases reported before the mid-20th century. Cases have been documented in several states, including Mexico, Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas, Hidalgo, Morelos, Oaxaca, San Luis Potosí, Sinaloa, and Puebla, with Puebla reporting the highest number of cases. Recent data is lacking, but a prevalence of 6% was reported in Atlixco (Puebla) using the Kato-Katz method. Peru: A 2007 review by Marcos and colleagues identified fascioliasis as an emerging disease in Peru, with 1,701 cases reported between 1963 and 2005. The data showed an increasing trend in cases, attributed to both improved detection and a genuine rise in infections. By 2010, human cases had been reported in 18 of Peru's 24 departments, while animal cases were documented in 21 departments. Prevalence rates varied, with 3% detected using unspecified methods, 24% using Kato-Katz, and up to 30% using Lumbreras rapid sedimentation. However, sampling for some studies occurred before 2007, and more recent data is limited. Diagnosis in Humans: Diagnosing fascioliasis is complex, with no standardized technique. Combining multiple diagnostic methods can improve accuracy but may be impractical for large-scale monitoring due to logistical and financial constraints. Microscopic techniques, such as detecting parasite eggs in feces, have low sensitivity, especially in cases of low infection intensity. The prepatent period (time between infection and egg shedding) is 3–4 months. Sensitivity can be improved by increasing the number of readings per sample or conducting repeated tests. Sedimentation-based microscopy techniques, such as Lumbreras rapid sedimentation, are more sensitive than flotation methods. Serological tests can detect infections 2–3 weeks post-infection, earlier than egg detection. However, these tests vary in performance, and many rely on crude antigens, affecting specificity and reliability. Antibody detection tests cannot differentiate between past and current infections, although an IgM ELISA (Fas2-ELISA) has been developed to distinguish acute from chronic infections. Serology is useful in areas where stool samples are difficult to obtain and can serve as a screening tool to identify potential cases for confirmation via microscopy or coproantigen tests. Coproantigen detection, such as the MM3-COPRO ELISA, identifies Fasciola antigens 6–8 weeks post-infection and becomes negative shortly after the infection clears. This method is sensitive and specific but does not quantify infection intensity. Molecular tests, while highly sensitive and specific, are expensive and do not detect infections during the prepatent period. Diagnosis in Animals: Animal fascioliasis is diagnosed based on clinical symptoms, seasonality, historical disease presence, and the presence of intermediate host snails. Confirmation can be achieved through microscopy, serology, or post-mortem liver inspection. Microscopy, particularly sedimentation techniques, is commonly used but may not always be reliable. Antibody detection tests are useful for herd-level prevalence studies but cannot differentiate between current and past infections. Coproantigen detection, such as MM3-COPRO, is sensitive and specific, detecting infections 4–8 weeks post-infection and correlating with parasite load. Treatment: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for treating fascioliasis in humans and animals. It is effective against both adult and juvenile parasites. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a single oral dose of 10 mg/kg. In cases of therapeutic failure or if deemed necessary by the treating physician, two doses of 10 mg/kg can be administered 12–24 hours apart. Nitazoxanide has shown inconsistent results in treating fascioliasis. Treatment effectiveness can be evaluated using microscopy 10–15 days post-treatment and repeated after 30 days. Serological tests are not recommended for assessing treatment efficacy, as antibody levels remain elevated after treatment. Elimination Efforts: The elimination of human fascioliasis as a public health problem requires a sustained prevalence of ≤5% (by coprology) without high-intensity infections (≥400 eggs per gram). The One Health approach, which integrates human, animal, and environmental health sectors, is essential for achieving this goal.g., treating domestic animals, controlling intermediate host snails), and community education. Operational plans for elimination should include identifying at-risk populations, securing political commitment, developing technical plans, and implementing coordinated activities across sectors. Monitoring and evaluation are critical to assess progress and make necessary adjustments.
